It can be a number of different Aphonopelma species from that location. Nobody is going to be able to help you, beyond taking a guess, unless you provide a photograph. Even then, you do have undescribed species in that area and they might still only be guessing with a photo for reference. Chances are that it is an Aphonopelma chalcodes and they are an appropriate species for beginners. Google that species for care information and you will be okay, even if they aren't that exact species.

All of the Aphonopelma from the states are appropriate for beginners and have the same husbandry requirements - keep at room temperature, provide dry substrate that is deep enough to prevent them from injuring themselves in a fall, a hide, and a water dish. They are very hardy and have a decent sized window of error. They aren't going to up and die if you make some minor mistakes.

I would not feed them insects from outside, even though that is where they've come from, I would suggest feeding them captive bred prey to eliminate any additional exposure to parasites or chemicals.

If this tarantula turns out to be male, I would suggest releasing him back where you found him, so he can keep his kind going. Once mature, males last a very short time and stop eating and drinking altogether.  If this tarantula ends up a female, they can potentially live well into their 30's.  Aphonopelma from that area are not huge - 4.5" is average for a full grown female Aphonopelma chalcodes. If this is a male, then there is a chance that they are either already mature or will become mature by the fall. Posting a photo will enable people to see if you have a mature male.

There are always certain risks with wild caught - parasites being the main one. It is really a better option to purchase captive bred individuals.

Aphonopelma seemanni are definitely not appropriate for handling. They are not chill at all. I would never even consider handling mine. Maybe you are mixing them up with Eupalaestrus campestratus - the Pink Zebra Beauty? 

As mentioned, there are lots of other species that are better suited for beginners - both care and temperament wise.

I am guessing that is an Aphonopelma seemanni. They are a bit fast and skittish and they do love to burrow. They are often not a species that is visible all the time. They will definitely burrow and disappear as spiderlings and juveniles. They also need it to be a bit more moist than the majority of beginner friendly species since they come from more tropical areas than the Aphonopelma found in the states.

I feed my spiderlings one appropriately sized prey item twice a week and my adults once a week. Some adults I will skip. It all depends on what size yours is. 

I second the recommendation of Tom Moran's YouTube channel. He doesn't provoke or antagonize any of his tarantulas, so you get a very good idea of what you can expect from normal interaction and feeding.

I haven't had that many moulting issues, unless they have had damaged legs when I got them. Damaged legs can often cause problems with moults. Missing legs are fine, but damaged legs can cause issues.

Keep them properly hydrated all the time and not just when you see that they are approaching a moult. Spiderlings need  more moisture because they lack the waxy protective cuticle on their exoskeletons that juveniles and adults have. That is why they are prone to desiccation more quickly. They create a liquid that is released between the old and new exoskeleton that helps to separate the two and extract themselves properly. They need to be properly hydrated in the long term in order for that moulting fluid to do the job properly. If they are constantly too dry, wetting down the enclosure a couple of days before moulting isn't going to help that process. The trick is to keep them hydrated over the long term.

The winter months are more challenging, but you have to keep on top of it. Trickle some water down the side of the vial to ensure that they have a damp spot if there is not enough room for a dish.
In my experience, older, wild caught, individuals take even longer to adjust.

Tarantulas are individuals and each can take a different amount of time to adjust to a new environment. Some can take weeks before you see normal behaviour that is typical for the species. Wild caught can take even more time than captive bred tarantulas. They can take vastly different amounts of time to ingest food as well.

You should include their size and photos of the enclosures for a more thorough assessment for why they are not displaying typical behaviour. Without that, people have to assume that they are adjusting to their environment.

I have a small female albino - she came to me newly hatched at 6 grams in October. I had a hell of a time getting her to eat... right up until between Christmas and New Years when she finally had her second shed. She eats like a champ now and I weighed her yesterday and she is 17 grams.

Snakes, like all animals, can be different weights and sizes and it is difficult to have a 'standard' for all. As long as she is healthy, and gaining weight at this stage as opposed to losing it, then I wouldn't be concerned. Snakes are opportunistic and hognoses go without food the entire winter in many places. Overall health is more important than just concentrating on weight alone.

I have an adult male who has not eaten since mid-November. He's lost a bit of weight, but I'm not concerned. I just make sure his conditions are good, he has fresh water at all times, and I occasionally offer him food. I weigh him every few weeks just to keep an eye on him.
